meta.title: Who really said "Computers are useless. They can only give you answers"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Picasso did say it - but not like this. Fifield's 1964 Paris Review interview has "But they are useless," said of "mechanical brains." "Computers" came later.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Computers are useless. They can only give you answers'?
meta.ogDescription: The 1964 Paris Review text reads "But they are useless. They can only give you answers" - about calculating machines. The word "computers" was added in 1982.

answer.label: Not Picasso’s exact words — a 1980s rewrite
answer.authorDates: 1881–1973 · Spanish painter and sculptor, co-founder of Cubism
answer.sourceLine: Picasso did say something very close, and it was written down — but not like this. William Fifield’s Paris Review interview of Summer–Fall 1964 records him remarking, of “the enormous new mechanical brains or calculating machines,” “But they are useless. They can only give you answers.” The word computers appears nowhere in that text; Fifield swapped it in himself in his 1982 book In Search of Genius, and the crisp, de-pronouned sentence spread through reviews, quotation books and magazine quizzes during the 1980s.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed wording, not disputed speaker — the remark is Picasso’s as recorded, but this exact sentence is a later editor’s tidy-up.

source.heading: Where the wording actually comes from

docMeta.dd: The Paris Review no. 32, Summer–Fall 1964 — article begins p. 37, remark on p. 62

source.excerpt: I feel I am nibbling on the edges of this world when I am capable of getting what Picasso means when he says to me—perfectly straight-facedly—later of the enormous new mechanical brains or calculating machines: “But they are useless. They can only give you answers.” How easy and comforting to take these things for jokes—boutades!
trail: Summer–Fall 1964 — the remark first reaches print in William Fifield’s composite interview in The Paris Review no. 32, article beginning p. 37, quote on p. 62. Picasso is speaking of “mechanical brains or calculating machines,” and the sentence begins “But they are useless” (Garson O’Toole’s ADS-L posting, with the passage verbatim ↗).
1967 — the poet Louis Zukofsky folds it into “A”-18, ascribing to “Pablo” the line “art begs disrespect, calculators can only give answers” — still calculators, not computers (Quote Investigator ↗).

1982–1983 — Fifield modernises his own vocabulary in In Search of Genius (Morrow): p. 40 gives “What good are computers? They can only give you answers,” while p. 145 reprints the Paris Review passage with “computers” substituted. A New York Times review on 13 February 1983 picked out the p. 145 version (Quote Investigator ↗).

Through the 1980s — the pronoun is dropped and the modern sentence takes hold. Wikiquote records its earliest known book appearance in Herman Feshbach’s essay in Man and Technology (1983), where the attribution is called “rumoured” (Wikiquote ↗); by May 1986 it was the answer to a magazine quiz question in Orange Coast (Quote Investigator ↗).
source.excerptNote: Fifield’s paragraph from The Paris Review no. 32, p. 62, transcribed from microfilm by Quote Investigator ↗. The magazine’s own online text of the article is cut off by its subscriber wall well before this passage.

source.rightsNote: Picasso’s remark survives only inside William Fifield’s account of it, and that account is modern: the article ran in The Paris Review no. 32 in 1964 and the book In Search of Genius was published by Morrow in 1982 — both far too recent for the US public domain. Treat the passage as a copyrighted text to be quoted and cited, not as free-standing public-domain wording.

author.heading: About Pablo Picasso
author.metaLine: 1881–1973 · Spanish painter and sculptor, co-founder of Cubism
author.bio: Pablo Picasso was born in Málaga in 1881 and spent most of his working life in France, where he co-founded Cubism and pioneered collage and constructed sculpture. By the early 1960s he was living at Mougins and had become famously hard to reach — Fifield’s piece is a composite — a number of interviews he did with Picasso, with his own observations threaded through. He died at Mougins in 1973, which is why every version of this quotation rests entirely on what someone else wrote down.

cite.sourceCitation: William Fifield, “Pablo Picasso—A Composite Interview,” The Paris Review no. 32 (Summer–Fall 1964), article beginning p. 37, quote at p. 62 — where the wording is “But they are useless. They can only give you answers,” said of “the enormous new mechanical brains or calculating machines.” The “computers” wording appears later, in Fifield’s In Search of Genius (New York: Morrow, 1982), pp. 40 and 145.

copyAttribution: Often quoted as "Computers are useless. They can only give you answers." What William Fifield actually printed, in The Paris Review no. 32 (Summer–Fall 1964), p. 62, was Picasso saying of "the enormous new mechanical brains or calculating machines": "But they are useless. They can only give you answers." The word "computers" was introduced by Fifield himself in In Search of Genius (Morrow, 1982); the polished modern sentence spread during the 1980s. — Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Right man, rewritten sentence
misattribution.intro: This is not a case of a quote pinned on the wrong person. Picasso really did say it, to a writer who published it in his lifetime. What travelled is a tidied-up version — three separate edits away from the words on the page.

items.why: Quote Investigator states plainly that “the word ‘computer’ did not actually appear in the text written by Fifield.” The 1964 article has Picasso speaking of “the enormous new mechanical brains or calculating machines”; Fifield substituted “computers” when he reused the passage in In Search of Genius (Quote Investigator ↗).

The recorded sentence starts with a pronoun — “But they are useless” — and QI notes only that the 1964 phrasing “used a pronoun for the pivotal referent; hence, it was not self-contained.” Nobody has dated the swap itself. The de-pronouned version is in circulation by 1983, Wikiquote’s earliest known book appearance being Herman Feshbach’s essay in Man and Technology (Wikiquote ↗), and QI finds it as a quiz answer in Orange Coast, May 1986 (Quote Investigator ↗).

items.who: William Fifield, In Search of Genius, p. 40
items.why: The same book carries a different opening on an earlier page: “He said contemptuously: ‘What good are computers? They can only give you answers.’ ” That prefatory question is not in the Paris Review text at all, so Fifield left two competing records of the same remark (Quote Investigator ↗).

The poet ascribed the line to “Pablo” in a section of his long poem published in 1967, choosing calculators — probably from the “calculating machines” phrasing in the magazine. It is a paraphrase of Fifield’s text, not an independent witness to Picasso (Quote Investigator ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Best available verdict: the remark is genuinely Picasso’s as recorded by Fifield — only the famous wording is not. Quote Investigator’s suggested careful rendering is “[As Pablo Picasso said of computers]: But they are useless. They can only give you answers,” and QI calls the popular version merely “semantically a reasonable match” to what Fifield wrote down (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why this one keeps getting sharper
lead: The line is a small case study in how quotations improve themselves. Fifield’s original is a writer’s aside, buried mid-paragraph and hedged with the observation that it would be “easy and comforting to take these things for jokes.” It leans on a pronoun, it names a technology nobody calls by that name any more, and it is impossible to put on a slide. Each later version fixes one of those problems: Fifield modernised the noun, a reviewer picked the cleaner of his two versions, and somewhere in the 1980s an editor deleted the pronoun and produced the three-word opening everyone now recites.

The irony is that the tidying is exactly what the remark is about. A quotation that survives by being rounded off into something more usable is a quotation being handed an answer rather than a question. Quote Investigator’s 2011 dig into it was prompted by an email from Kevin Kelly of Wired, who had noticed that Fifield’s own book carried two different versions of the same sentence — the first crack in what had looked like a settled quotation (Quote Investigator ↗).
context.detailsSummary: The three competing versions, side by side
detailsBody: The Paris Review no. 32, Summer–Fall 1964, p. 62 — “…later of the enormous new mechanical brains or calculating machines: ‘But they are useless. They can only give you answers.’ ” This is the earliest evidence located by Quote Investigator, verified on microfilm.

In Search of Genius, Morrow, 1982, p. 40 — “He said contemptuously: ‘What good are computers? They can only give you answers.’ ” Fifield adds that he thought it the most significant single thing he ever heard Picasso say.

In Search of Genius, Morrow, 1982, p. 145 — the Paris Review paragraph again, with “of computers” in place of the machines. This is the version a New York Times reviewer reprinted on 13 February 1983, and the version The Yale Book of Quotations (2006) cites.

schema.verdictNote: Pablo Picasso made the remark, as recorded by William Fifield in The Paris Review no. 32 (Summer–Fall 1964), where it reads “But they are useless. They can only give you answers,” said of “the enormous new mechanical brains or calculating machines.” The familiar “Computers are useless” wording is Fifield’s own 1982 rewrite in In Search of Genius, further tidied during the 1980s — nobody is falsely credited, only the words are not the recorded ones.
